There can of course be no doubt that what we are dealing with here are advanced products of the decay of the original conception of philosophy.
So when Hegel attacks these phenomena and insists on the active, living character of philosophy, he is simply restoring the authentic philosophical tradition.
But as we already know, he also introduces something fundamentally new into it: the idea that philosophy and wisdom are, by their very nature, a collective undertaking.
Naturally, this innovation also changes our idea of the moral conduct of the “sage.”
It is no longer enough for him to ignore public opinion. The “sage” lives in a genuinely ethical way if and only if the surrounding world finds his life “understandable” and “satisfactory.”
His private recognition of his own moral perfection is no longer sufficient. What is required is collective, public, and ultimately political recognition by the State.
It is, of course, just as correct to understand the practical side of philosophy collectively and historically as it is to understand its theoretical side in the same way.
For that reason, both sides of Hegel’s conception passed into Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism.

But just as the individualist conception of Socrates and Plato was later distorted, especially in Roman times, so the collectivist conception of Hegel and Marx underwent a very similar distortion in the form of the vulgar “sociologism” that appeared in the West during the nineteenth century.
Two opposite conclusions can be drawn from the obvious inadequacy of the principle of being “true to oneself.”

The first is to say that anything is moral as long as some existing society or State recognizes it as moral. Whenever a private individual comes into conflict with public morality, the individual must always be wrong.
From this standpoint, the philosopher’s morality consists in nothing more than conforming to commonly accepted norms. Political and social conformism then becomes the only possible ethical attitude.
But the very same starting point can lead directly to the opposite conclusion.
That is the conclusion Hegel drew.

If ethical life requires collective, social, and political recognition, and if I believe my own life to be ethical, then I am obliged to do everything in my power to change social and political conditions for as long as society and the State refuse to agree with my judgment of my own life.
Instead of inactive or “passive” conformism, we therefore arrive at an active revolutionary spirit.
It is true that Hegel himself believed the ideal State had already been created in his time, so he saw no need to adopt a revolutionary attitude toward his own present.
But when it came to the past—that is, when he was dealing not with “wisdom” but precisely with philosophy—he did defend a revolutionary conception of ethics.
As is well known, world history was for him the “court of judgment of the world,” whose final verdict is delivered in accordance with the final sociopolitical ideal.

Ultimately, therefore, everything that contributed to reaching that ideal was ethical. And so too was everything that came into conflict with the existing historical order, at least insofar as that conflict moved things forward.

It is precisely this idea of the “court of world history” that separates authentic Hegelianism—the close relative of the revolutionary socialism of Marx, Lenin, and Stalin—from conformist sociologism.

It is interesting to notice that the ethical side of this collectivist and historical Hegelian-Marxist conception, just like its theoretical side, was quietly prepared not by pagan philosophy but by Christian and theological pseudo-philosophy.
Christianity rejected from the outset the absurd principle of being “true to oneself.”
Human beings were not the measure of morality. God was—and in practice that meant the Church and its representative, the priest.
Every person had to answer, in confession, every question concerning the moral side of his life.
The Christian “saint,” corresponding to the philosophical “sage,” therefore had to live in such a way that his answers would always be “understandable” and “satisfactory.”
There can be no doubt that this conception is mistaken because of its theological theism.
But it is equally undeniable that, compared with the way pagan and individualist philosophy posed the moral question, it represents a step forward.

All that is needed is to replace the idea of the “divine tribunal” with Hegel’s idea of the “tribunal of history”—that is, the judgment of humanity as a whole—and then replace the Church and the priest with the “ideal” State and the representatives of civil society.
Once these substitutions are made, the Christian conception becomes a revolutionary and socialist one: the conception that goes back to Hegel and is now represented by Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism.
In short, make these changes and we find ourselves directly within Soviet practices such as “public oversight,” “reporting to the Party,” “collective discussion,” and so on.
The concept of “wisdom,” and therefore of philo-sophy understood as the striving for “wisdom,” necessarily includes a moral and active dimension.

In striving for “wisdom,” the philosopher strives to reach a position in which he can answer meaningfully—that is, “understandably”—and convincingly—that is, “satisfactorily”—every question that can be put to him.
And he must be able to answer not merely privately, to himself and within himself, but openly, before himself and before the world.
This means that he must actively contribute to creating the sociopolitical conditions in which his own ethical ideal will also be the ideal of all humanity.

And these turn out to be precisely the conditions under which he can reach his theoretical ideal of “wisdom”—that is, the conditions under which he can genuinely know how to answer every question concerning himself.
The same conditions that make it possible for him to answer privately, in petto, also allow him to answer openly before the world without “embarrassment” and without “fear.”
This conception, which crowns the development of the philosophical tradition, was first formulated by Hegel.

When it passed from Hegel into Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism, it was merely clarified and developed on one point that is now perfectly clear to us: which sociopolitical conditions make possible the wisdom toward which every philosopher must strive?

Those conditions, as we know, will be fulfilled by the future communist society, which will crown and complete the historical development of humanity and already exists today as a real possibility—“in potential”—in the form of the Communist Party.

Having established this, we can now say that, in our time, to call oneself a philosopher—to strive for “wisdom”—while refusing to take an active part in building a Communist Party capable of governing, and refusing to take an active part in bringing communist society into existence, is as absurd as wanting to become a great swimmer while refusing to get into the water and learn how to swim.
One final point must be added.

If our claim is correct, as the book itself will demonstrate, then the ultimate goal of human existence in communist society is nothing other than complete self-awareness—that is, the “wisdom” toward which philosophy strives.

In other words, someone who takes part in the communist project but refuses to study philosophy and its Marxist-Leninist-Stalinist culmination is like another would-be swimmer who has indeed jumped into the water, but once he gets into the deep end forgets that he came there to learn to swim and not simply to splash around.
We can end our first chapter here.
Before moving to the next one, however, we need to draw one further essential conclusion from what has already been said.
We have seen that the philosopher is obliged to take an active part in the preparatory but real work aimed at bringing communist society into existence.
First, because this society is a necessary condition of his own philosophical ideal, in the narrow sense of the word.
Second, because communist society will never come into existence “by itself.”

The doctrine of Lenin and Stalin, in agreement with Hegel and Marx, clearly exposed the falsity of that vulgar misunderstanding of Marxism according to which certain “iron laws” supposedly carry history “necessarily” toward the victory of socialism.
If those “iron laws” are good for anything, they are especially useful to our Western social democrats, who can entrust everything to them while sitting comfortably by the roadside and doing nothing.
The falsity of this doctrine is repeatedly confirmed in spectacular fashion by events themselves.

Without the active and revolutionary intervention of the Party that strives toward communism, these “iron laws” may certainly lead to an “iron society,” but hardly to anything resembling the promised socialist and communist society.
Since this is so, anyone who regards communist society as his ideal has a duty to devote all his strength to reaching that goal.
The goal may be logically necessary, but in actual fact it becomes possible only through conscious and active effort.
And what is true in practice is equally true in theory.
The intellectual and cognitive development that corresponds to, depends on, and accompanies active creative development does not arise sponte sua either.
Here too, effort and work are required, along with struggle and a willingness to accept sacrifice and risk.
Without them, these two processes may simply stagnate, or they may fail in fact to reach the destination toward which they are logically supposed to move.
Philosophy can therefore genuinely perish and never reach its logical goal—wisdom—if no one actually takes the trouble to create the real and necessary conditions for reaching that goal.
Conversely, philosophy can also disappear if the people creating those conditions cease trying to “become conscious of themselves”—that is, if they stop asking questions about what they are doing.
Preventing this requires continuous effort, work, struggle, and readiness for every sacrifice and every risk.
And when the thinker undertakes this work, he does so not merely as a citizen but specifically as a philosopher in the narrow sense of the word.
Since the fundamental goal of his life is to acquire the art of asking questions and answering them, he must do everything in his power to ensure that this ability does not die with him.

It must be passed from one generation to the next until the creation of communist society—to which he himself has actively contributed—makes it possible to ask every question and answer every question meaningfully and convincingly.
A philosopher worthy of the name must therefore understand that he has to act and struggle not only as a citizen and a communist but also as a philosopher.
These are not two separate activities that happen to coexist in the same person. They are two aspects of one and the same life.
Comrade Stalin’s activity offers the clearest proof of this: not only does he always do, as a communist, what he says; he also always speaks, as a philosopher, about what he does.
II. Perfect knowledge as “wisdom,” that is, as the completion of conscious awareness
We have defined philosophy as the striving to attain “wisdom.”

Wisdom, in turn, has been defined as the ability to answer meaningfully and convincingly every question that a human being can ask himself, or that others can ask him, about his life and actions in the material world of space and time.

We also assume that human beings themselves, without any outside help and through their command of meaningful speech or logos, are capable, first, of formulating rigorously every question about themselves that can in principle be expressed verbally or “logically,” and second, of answering those questions using only ordinary or “normal,” discursive or “logical” and “rational” means.
“Wisdom” is human speech about humanity—an “anthropo-logy.” It is human speech about oneself.
To be a philosopher—that is, to strive for “wisdom”—therefore means striving toward complete self-awareness.
The development or “progress” of philosophy is nothing other than the development of self-consciousness: its gradual deepening and expansion until it reaches complete fulfillment in “wisdom.”
The “sage,” who possesses complete self-awareness or perfected self-consciousness, actually and definitively knows about himself everything that it is logically possible to know.
Let us now examine what kind of knowledge, or consciousness, is required for complete self-awareness and perfected self-consciousness.
What, in general, must we know?
What kinds of questions must we be able to answer if we are to possess complete knowledge of ourselves—if we are to answer every question about ourselves?
What, in the final analysis, must a human being know in order to possess complete knowledge of humanity?
We have already noted that the saying “know yourself,” uttered by one of the seven “sages” of ancient Greece, can be regarded as the source of all the decisive reflections of philosophy.
We can now add that this same injunction echoes at the beginning of the three great “classical” periods in the history of philo-sophy.
Socrates and Plato began from it, and in doing so determined the entire development of “pagan” Greek philosophy through to its culmination in Neoplatonism.
Augustine repeated these words when he laid down the basic principles of Christian philosophy.
And finally, they stood at the center of Descartes’ reflections, through which he established the principle of “modern” philosophy—a philosophy that would later reach its summit in Hegel.
Hegel’s doctrine openly and consciously identifies philosophy with human discourse about humanity: with the complete disclosure and final perfection of self-consciousness.
Leaving Plato and Augustine aside, we will concentrate on Descartes and Hegel.
Let us examine what, from their point of view, a person must know in order to answer satisfactorily the question about himself.

Like every philosopher, Descartes wanted certain knowledge—“truth,” or epistēmē—as opposed to opinions accepted merely on faith: prejudice, or doxa. To reach it, he used a method that is actually quite common in philosophy, as we will see: doubt, or “methodical skepticism.”

He decided to doubt the truth of everything he had previously accepted without sufficient grounds, simply because he had heard it from others or become used to believing it. As he pushed this method further, he concluded that strictly speaking we can doubt almost anything, even the existence of the world. After all, we cannot be completely certain that what appears to us while awake is fundamentally different from what appears to us in a dream or under the influence of a drug.
There is only one thing we cannot doubt: doubt itself.

To doubt means to doubt the “truth” of something and, in the end, to doubt whether what we are doubting really exists. But doubting the existence of doubt is obviously absurd. To doubt doubt is still to doubt. In other words, the very act of denying doubt confirms that doubt exists.
Doubt itself is therefore completely beyond doubt.
